So like the title says, I messed up my ext4 filesystem somehow. It wouldn't let me traverse directories due to errors. fsck refuses to fix them automatically. Being the typical lazy, adventurous (read: dumb) user I am, I wrote this expect script and executed it:

#!/usr/bin/expect

set timeout 30
spawn e2fsck /dev/sda4
while {0==0} {
 expect "<y>? "
 send "\n"
}

It's still running. There were a ton of errors apparently. How screwed am I?

Edit: A friend has brought to my attention that my solution is actually horribly over-engineered. e2fsck has a -y option (always assume yes) to do this for me. Derp.
I corrupted my filesystem. fsck will repair it automatically whether it wants to or not.
Lol. I don't think anyone can say how much damage has been done without getting more information. That being said, I don't know enough to provide the needed commands to find said information.
I can tell you how much damage was done. When the fsck completed, my entire user directory (266 GB of data) was in lost+found. I was able to recover very little from it. Most of it is garbage now.
It's amazing you managed to do that kind of damage to an ext filesystem. The only way I've ever destroyed one was with a magnet.

e2fsck has a -y option

True, but this taught you something, yes? If so, then it's not a wasted experience.

Also: when ext4 screws up, it usually screws up big, but in such a way that fsck can fix it, but you definitely want to go with the -y option, because otherwise you'll be sitting there all night.

The fsck ran for at least half an hour. The end result was not what I was hoping for. See my reply to that other guy's comment for details.

But yeah, I learned loads today. I think the reason it got corrupted was due to my adjusting the partition table to get it ready for a new distro. One issue led to another, and seven hours later I have a working system again.

Ouch. Yeah, there's not a tried and true safe way to "shrink" an ext4 partition the way that Windows "shrinks" FAT32 or NTFS. The only foolproof method is to copy data from the source partition to another, smaller partition, but that's usually not a good fit for people who want to stick a separate OS on their primary drive.

Sorry that you wound up in a bad state with lost&found... maybe there's a way for you to get some of the most important stuff back, if you're willing to go through it.

That was the method I used to recover the little bit I could recover. A lot of the data really was just garbled though. None of my most important directories survived.

Edit: The weird thing is I didn't even modify that partition. It was the important one. The other three, yeah. I deleted and recreated them a few times. I made it a point not to screw with home though.
